purpose: Show how a developer decides whether a web feature can be used: shared support data, support tables, then a runtime feature check.
explanation: MDN browser-compat-data feeds MDN support tables; its README lists caniuse among projects using the data, and caniuse also uses its own Fyrd/caniuse data (caniuse About). You read the tables to plan. At runtime, feature detection (MDN guide, 'The concept of feature detection') runs the enhanced code when the feature exists and the fallback code when it does not.
alt: Flowchart: support data from browser-compat-data and caniuse feeds MDN and caniuse support tables; then a decision Feature detected in this browser? leads to enhanced code on yes and fallback code on no.

learning_check.question: A support table says a feature works in 90% of browsers. Why does your code still need a runtime check?
learning_check.answer: Tables describe browsers in general; the user's own browser may be old or partial, so feature detection picks the enhanced or fallback path at runtime.

title: From support data to a runtime feature check
The three Baseline statuses over time
purpose: See how a web feature moves from limited availability to newly available to widely available.
explanation: A feature starts as Limited availability. When every core browser supports it, it becomes Newly available on the newly interoperable date. After 30 months it becomes Widely available. The status changes only because of support and time.
alt: Flowchart with three boxes in a row: Limited availability, then Newly available when all core browsers ship the feature, then Widely available after 30 months.

learning_check.question: A feature became Newly available in December 2023. In which month does it become Widely available?
learning_check.answer: June 2026, which is 30 months after December 2023.

title: Three ways to test a feature, one decision
purpose: See that different tests all end in the same choice between enhanced code and fallback code.
explanation: A page can test a feature with the CSS @supports rule, with CSS.supports() in JavaScript, or with the in operator on an object. Each test answers yes or no. Yes runs the enhanced code. No runs the fallback code, so the page still works.
alt: Flowchart: a page loads, then one of three tests runs (@supports, CSS.supports, in operator), all joining one supported question that leads to enhanced code on yes and fallback code on no.

learning_check.question: Which test needs no JavaScript?
learning_check.answer: The @supports rule, because it is written in CSS.

title: Browser Compat Data: module map
purpose: See the five parts of the repository and how a support claim moves from its schema to an app.
explanation: The schema defines one support claim. The linter checks files against it. The build resolves mirror values and writes data.json. CI and release publish it, and apps then query the tree. Evidence: lint/lint.js:127-160 and scripts/build/index.js:248-257 at 8f942b4.
alt: Flowchart of five modules: schema-and-types feeds data-linter and build-pipeline, the linter feeds the build, the build feeds build-and-infra for release and consumer-api for querying.

learning_check.question: Which module turns the string mirror into a real version number?
learning_check.answer: build-pipeline, in scripts/build/mirror.js, not the consumer code.

title: Browser Compat Data: from edit to app
purpose: Follow one support claim from a contributor's edit through lint, build and publish to an app's query.
explanation: A contributor edits JSON and the linter rejects bad claims. The build resolves mirror values through mirror.js, validates the result and writes data.json. The release workflow publishes the build folder. An app imports data.json and walks it. Evidence: scripts/build/index.js:284-290 and .github/workflows/release.yml:63 at 8f942b4.
alt: Sequence diagram: contributor edits and lints, build calls the mirror step and writes data.json, the release workflow publishes the build folder, and an app imports and queries the data.

learning_check.question: Where do mirror values get replaced by numbers: in the source file or in the published file?
learning_check.answer: In the published data.json; the source files keep the string mirror.

title: TC39 proposal stages from 0 to 4
purpose: See that a JavaScript proposal can change until Stage 4, so a tutorial about an earlier stage can go out of date.
explanation: The TC39 process document lists six stages by number: 0, 1, 2, 2.7, 3 and 4. Only Stage 0 has a name, strawperson; the other labels in the timeline are descriptions, not official names. A proposal can change or stop before Stage 4. Stage 4 needs four things: two compatible implementations that pass Test262, significant in-the-field experience with shipping implementations, a pull request with the integrated spec text, and editor sign-off. Rely on a feature only at Stage 4, and then check browser support.
alt: Timeline of six TC39 stages by number, from Stage 0 (strawperson, an idea) through Stages 1, 2, 2.7 and 3 to Stage 4, where the feature joins the standard, so only Stage 4 features are part of the standard.

learning_check.question: A tutorial teaches a Stage 2 proposal. Why can its code break later?
learning_check.answer: At Stage 2 the spec text is a draft, so the syntax can still change or the proposal can stop before Stage 4.

title: Test the feature, then pick a code path
purpose: See how a feature test picks the enhanced or the fallback code path in each browser.
explanation: Feature detection asks the browser what it can do at run time and branches on the answer, so every visitor gets a working page.
alt: A page tests a feature before it uses it. The @supports rule tests CSS in CSS, CSS.supports runs the same test in JavaScript, and the in operator checks that an object such as navigator has a member such as geolocation. A true answer runs the enhanced code, a false answer runs the fallback code. Some features cannot be tested, so pages load polyfills, and the polyfill.io takeover in 2024 shows that third-party polyfill code runs with your page. Origin trials turn an experimental feature on with a token until the trial expires, so the fallback must stay.

learning_check.question: A browser has no Geolocation API. What does the code if ("geolocation" in navigator) { … } else { … } run?
learning_check.answer: The else branch, which offers static maps, because the in test returns false.

timeline.heading: Test the feature, not the browser

title: How a feature moves from Limited to Widely available
purpose: See which two inputs set a feature's Baseline label: support in every core browser, and the months since that day.
explanation: Only two inputs move the Baseline label: whether every core browser supports the feature, and how many months have passed since the last one shipped it.
alt: Baseline gives each web feature one label. It checks seven core browsers: Chrome on desktop and Android, Edge, Firefox on desktop and Android, and Safari on macOS and iOS. While any one of them lacks the feature, the label is Limited availability. When the last one ships it, the feature is Newly available. Thirty months later it is Widely available, as the :has() selector shows: Newly available in December 2023, Widely available in June 2026. Can I use shows the support of each browser with four colors. Widely available means most sites, not all.

learning_check.question: A feature works in six of the seven core browsers and has existed for five years. Which Baseline label does it have, and why?
learning_check.answer: Limited availability, because the 30-month clock starts only when the last core browser ships the feature.

title: Move a feature through the Baseline labels
purpose: Predict a feature's Baseline label from its core-browser support and the months since it became Newly available.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict a feature's Baseline label from its core-browser support and the months since it became Newly available.
alt: A guided walkthrough of the Baseline lifecycle, paused for predictions, and a stepper with seven core-browser cells. Highlighted cells are browsers that support the feature. The learner adds browsers one by one and runs the 30-month clock, and watches the label move from Limited availability to Newly available to Widely available. The :has() selector, Newly available in December 2023, is the worked example. A last question reads the Can I use color legend.

learning_check.question: A feature works in six of the seven core browsers. Which Baseline label does it have?
learning_check.answer: Limited availability. Baseline has no partial step. While any one core browser lacks the feature, the label is Limited availability. Only the last core browser to ship it moves the label to Newly available.

title: Baseline checker execution flow
purpose: Show how the checker turns a feature path into a Limited, Newly or Widely label.
explanation: main.ts passes each feature path to checkFeature. It reads the feature from the BCD tree and each core browser's support. One missing browser gives Limited. Otherwise the latest release date is the interoperable date, and classify applies the 30-month rule.
alt: Flowchart: main.ts passes feature paths to checkFeature. getFeature reports an ERROR line for a bad path. supportFor returns Limited early when any core browser says no. interoperableDate gives Unknown when a release date is missing; otherwise classify returns Newly or Widely by the 30-month rule.

learning_check.question: One core browser has no support for a feature. What status does the checker print, and why?
learning_check.answer: Limited, because Baseline needs all core browsers to support a feature before it can be Newly or Widely.

title: Switch a browser feature on and off
purpose: Predict which code path a feature test runs when the browser has or lacks the feature.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict which code path a feature test runs when the browser has or lacks the feature.
alt: A guided walkthrough of three feature tests from MDN (@supports, CSS.supports and the in operator), paused for predictions, plus a simulated browser where the learner switches subgrid, geolocation or an origin-trial feature on and off and steps through the test to see whether the enhanced or the fallback code runs. It ends with the polyfill.io risk and why an expired origin trial still needs the fallback.

learning_check.question: This browser has no Geolocation API. Which code runs?
learning_check.answer: The else branch, which offers static maps. "geolocation" in navigator only asks whether navigator has that member. Here it returns false, so the else branch runs and the visitor gets static maps instead of a broken page.

title: The path to a first open source contribution
purpose: See the order in which a newcomer orients in a project and reaches a pull request, and when an issue comes first.
explanation: The GitHub Open Source Guide orders the path. The README explains the project and the CONTRIBUTING file explains how to help. The issue tracker shows current work. A small fix, such as a typo, goes straight to a pull request. A bigger change starts with a comment or an issue, and the pull request follows after discussion. Maintainers then review it.
alt: Flowchart: Read README, then Read CONTRIBUTING, then Search issue tracker. A small fix goes straight to Open pull request; a bigger change goes first to Comment or open issue, then to the pull request when agreed. The pull request ends at Maintainer review.

learning_check.question: You want to add a new option to a library you use. Do you open a pull request first?
learning_check.answer: No. A bigger change starts with a comment or an issue so the maintainers can agree first; only small fixes such as a typo go straight to a pull request.

title: Share button decision flow
purpose: Show how the Share button picks the Web Share API, the clipboard, or a visible link.
explanation: main.ts passes navigator to shareOrCopy. hasShare is tested first with the in operator. If sharing is missing or fails, hasClipboard is tested. If the clipboard is missing or rejected, the page shows a selectable link. A closed share sheet ends as cancelled.
alt: Flowchart: the click handler calls shareOrCopy, which tests hasShare and calls navigator.share, then falls back to hasClipboard and clipboard.writeText, and last to a visible link; AbortError ends as cancelled.

learning_check.question: Why does shareOrCopy test for navigator.share instead of the browser name?
learning_check.answer: A member test stays correct as browsers change, and it picks the fallback only where the feature is missing.

title: Step through Preact's createElement
purpose: Practice reading one real library function and predicting what it returns.
explanation: Preact's createElement (src/create-element.js:16-33 @ 34b99c6) copies props into a new object, but moves key out, and moves ref out when the type is not a function component. One child stays a single value; two or more become an array. Then createVNode builds the virtual node.
alt: Code walkthrough of createElement in four steps: signature, a loop that splits key and ref from the props, children handling, and the hand-over to createVNode, so key never reaches the props.

learning_check.question: You call createElement('a', { href: '/docs', key: 'nav' }, 'Docs'). What are the vnode props?
learning_check.answer: { href: '/docs', children: 'Docs' }: key moves to the vnode, and one child stays a single value.

purpose: Show the four layers of the TIL learning journal and which depends on which.
explanation: The interface calls the application use cases, which call domain rules and ports. Infrastructure implements the ports. main.tsx creates and wires every object. The Baseline status rule in BaselineCalculator comes from mini project 1 and the browser-compat-data takeaways.
alt: Layer diagram: main.tsx wires the interface, application, domain and infrastructure objects. Interface depends on application, application on domain, and infrastructure implements the domain ports.

learning_check.question: Why does the domain layer not import LocalStorageNoteRepository?
learning_check.answer: The domain declares the NoteRepository port and infrastructure implements it, so rules stay testable without a browser.

title: TIL journal layers

purpose: Show what happens when the learner saves a note, including the failure path.
explanation: NoteForm calls AddNote, which asks NoteValidator to check the draft. An invalid draft throws ValidationError and the form shows a focused alert list. For a valid draft, AddNote asks ReviewScheduler for the first review date, saves the note through LocalStorageNoteRepository, and returns the note to NoteForm.
alt: Sequence diagram: Learner presses Save; NoteForm calls AddNote; AddNote calls NoteValidator. On invalid input the form shows an alert. Otherwise AddNote asks ReviewScheduler for the first review date, the repository saves the note, AddNote returns the note to NoteForm, and the form shows a status line.

learning_check.question: Where does the first review date come from?
learning_check.answer: AddNote asks ReviewScheduler.first(today) after validation, and the form shows it in the status line.

title: Saving a note, with the failure path

purpose: Show how the app is built and served as static files.
explanation: npm run data reads the compat data package once and writes a small JSON snapshot. vite build bundles the app with the VITE_ variables into static files. Any static host serves them; the browser keeps notes in localStorage.
alt: Flowchart: the compat data package feeds feature-snapshot.json, which with the VITE_ variables goes into vite build, then a static file host, then the browser with localStorage.

learning_check.question: Why is @mdn/browser-compat-data not in the production dependencies?
learning_check.answer: Only the snapshot file ships; the package is used at development time, so it stays out of the bundle and the production audit.
